transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. I'm Dr. [Name]. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Hi, doctor. Yeah… I guess what finally pushed me to come in is that I just can’t seem to organize all the moving parts anymore.

I work as a software developer, and there are all these separate threads I’m supposed to keep straight—patent notes, workshop preparation, gallery deadlines, decisions I need to make with the team—and it’s like I can see all of them, but I can’t reliably sort them into “this matters most” versus “this is just making the most noise right now.” So I end up reacting to whatever is loudest or most urgent-feeling in the moment, even if, objectively, that’s not the thing that should be first.

It’s frustrating because I’m not trying to avoid things, and I’m not unaware that they’re important. It’s more like the system in my head for lining them up and moving through them has gotten… messy, I guess. I’ll start one thing, then remember another, then switch because that one feels more pressing, and by the end I’ve been busy but not necessarily effective. That’s the part that made me think I should talk to someone instead of just trying to push through it again.
Have you noticed any changes in your mood lately, like feeling down, hopeless, or losing interest in things you usually enjoy?

I’m not sure I’d say that, exactly. I mean, I get frustrated with myself, definitely, and sometimes I feel worn down by the constant sense that I’m behind or not steering things very well. But “down” or “hopeless” feels stronger than what I’ve noticed.

And I don’t think I’ve lost interest in things in the usual sense. It’s more that when everything feels scattered, even things I normally enjoy can start to feel like one more thing in the pile, if that makes sense. But I still care about them. I still want to do them. I just sometimes don’t get to them cleanly, or I arrive at them mentally cluttered.

So… I guess my answer is, no major mood change that I’ve clearly noticed. More stress and frustration than sadness, I think.

Can you describe how you handle tasks or responsibilities outside of work—like household chores, personal projects, or even planning social events? Do you find similar challenges with staying organized or prioritizing those?

Yes, it’s pretty similar outside of work, honestly. Maybe the specific tasks are different, but the pattern feels the same.

Like with things around the house or personal projects, I’ll have several things sitting in my head at once, and I have trouble sorting out what actually needs to happen first. It’s not that I don’t know the chores or responsibilities exist. I can see all the pieces, almost too many of them. But then whatever feels loudest in the moment grabs me.

So I might start dealing with one thing because it suddenly feels urgent, and then I remember something else I meant to do, and then that pulls me away. And by the end I’ve technically been doing things, but I haven’t necessarily done the thing that mattered most or finished the thing I started.

That’s really the part that pushed me to come in. At work it shows up with patent notes, workshop prep, gallery deadlines, team decisions—all these moving parts—and outside work it’s the same basic problem of not being able to organize and prioritize them reliably. It feels like I’m constantly reacting instead of deciding.
Can you recall a time in the past few weeks when you felt genuinely pleased or satisfied with something, even a small thing?

Hmm… I’m not sure I can pull up a really clear example right away. Not because nothing good has happened, exactly, but I don’t think I’ve been stopping long enough to notice that “pleased” feeling very cleanly.

Maybe there have been small moments where I finished something and thought, okay, that went fine, or I felt a little relieved that it was done. But satisfied… I don’t know. I’d have to think about that more. It’s not like I’m walking around unable to enjoy anything, I just don’t have a specific recent moment jumping out at me when you ask it that way.
Do you find it difficult to sustain your attention during tasks or activities, even when they’re important or something you care about?

Yes. Very much, actually. And it’s frustrating because it’s not only with boring things or things I don’t care about. It happens with things I genuinely think are important, or even things I’m interested in.

With coding, for example, I can be in the middle of working through something where I really need to keep the whole structure in my head — like what I just changed, what I’m testing, what the next step is — and then Slack pings, or a browser tab catches my eye, or even just some visual idea pops into my head, like “oh, that layout could be cleaner,” and suddenly I’m gone. I don’t mean I glance away for five seconds and come back. I mean I can lose the entire thread of what I was doing.

Then I’ll realize twenty minutes later that I’ve been following some totally unrelated design rabbit hole, or reading something adjacent but not actually useful for the task I was supposed to be doing. And the annoying part is that in the moment it can feel vaguely connected, like I can justify it to myself as “this might matter,” but when I step back, it’s clearly not what I meant to be doing.

So yes, sustaining attention is difficult. It feels less like I’m choosing not to focus and more like the focus gets yanked sideways by whatever is most immediate or visually interesting or noisy at that second.
Do you often feel restless, as if you need to be moving or doing something, even when you're trying to relax or focus on a single task?

Yes, I do. It’s not always like I’m bouncing off the walls or anything, but there’s this physical pressure sometimes, like my body starts insisting that I need to move.

The clearest example is long design calls. I’ll be sitting there trying to look like I’m paying attention and staying engaged, and after a while I can feel this tension building up. It’s almost like I can’t stay settled in the chair anymore. I’ll start shifting around, then I’ll move to a different chair, then I’ll stand up, and pretty soon I’m pacing around my office with my headset on.

And I’m still trying to focus on the call—I’m not trying to wander off—but sitting still starts to feel weirdly uncomfortable, like it takes extra effort on top of actually listening. Sometimes I’ll catch myself arranging things on my desk or walking in circles just so I can keep myself from feeling trapped in the chair. So yes, even when I’m supposed to be relaxing or concentrating on one thing, there’s often this need to move or do something physically.
Have you found yourself acting on impulse or making decisions quickly without thinking them through, even if it led to problems later?

I’m not sure I’d describe that as a major pattern for me. I mean, I can make quick decisions sometimes, like anyone, especially if I’m tired or just trying to get something off my plate. But when you say “acting on impulse” in a way that leads to problems later, I don’t immediately think, yes, that’s me.

I’m trying to think of examples, and nothing obvious is coming to mind. I don’t tend to, like, suddenly spend a lot of money or make dramatic decisions out of nowhere, at least not that I can point to. If anything, with bigger decisions I probably get stuck thinking about them too much rather than jumping too fast.

There may be smaller moments where I’ll answer too quickly or click something or agree to something before I’ve fully thought through the timing, but I don’t know if that’s what you mean. It doesn’t feel like the main issue I run into, or at least it’s not one I’ve noticed causing serious problems later.
Have you noticed yourself becoming more irritable, easily annoyed, or emotionally reactive lately, even in situations where you wouldn't expect to react that way?

I don’t know that I’ve noticed that as a big change, honestly. I mean, I can get annoyed, sure, especially if I’m already stretched thin or something keeps interrupting me, but I’m not sure I’d say I’m suddenly more emotionally reactive lately in a way that feels out of character.

I’m trying to think of a specific example, and nothing really jumps out as, like, “wow, that was disproportionate.” Maybe there are moments where I’m shorter than I’d like to be, or I feel irritated faster than I’d prefer, but it doesn’t feel like the main thing I’ve been dealing with. It’s not like I’m having blowups or snapping at people constantly, at least not that I’m aware of.

I guess I’d say I’m not sure. If you mean just everyday frustration, then yes, I have that sometimes. But if you mean a noticeable pattern where I’m reacting much more strongly than the situation calls for, I don’t think I’ve really observed that.
Can you describe how you've been sleeping lately? Have you noticed any changes in your sleep, like trouble falling asleep, waking up frequently, or feeling tired even after a full night's rest?

I’m not totally sure how to answer that, because I haven’t been tracking my sleep in any careful way. I don’t have a clear “before and after” sense, like something suddenly changed and now I’m waking up every night or anything like that.

I mean, I do have nights where I don’t feel very rested, but I’m not sure whether that’s because of the sleep itself, or just normal life stuff, or not getting enough hours, or maybe just being mentally tired. I don’t want to overstate it and say, yes, I’m definitely having insomnia, because I don’t know that that’s true.

Falling asleep can vary, I guess, but I haven’t noticed a consistent pattern that stands out enough for me to say it’s a major problem. Same with waking up during the night—I’m sure it happens sometimes, but not in a way I’ve really been thinking of as a symptom. I probably should pay more attention to it, honestly, because if you asked me how many hours I got over the past week, I’d be estimating pretty wildly.

So… I’d say no major sleep change that I’ve clearly noticed. Maybe some tiredness here and there, but nothing I can confidently describe as a specific sleep problem.
Over the past few weeks, have you found it difficult to feel pleasure or interest in things, even activities you used to enjoy?

I don’t think so, at least not in a clear way. I’m trying to think about the last few weeks specifically, and I can’t say I’ve noticed that things feel flat or that I can’t enjoy anything anymore.

There are definitely times where I don’t get around to things I usually like, or I’ll sort of put them off, but I’m not sure that’s the same as not feeling pleasure from them. Like if I actually start doing something I enjoy, I can usually still get into it, at least somewhat. The harder part is sometimes just getting started or making space for it, but I don’t know that I’d describe it as losing interest.

So I guess my answer is no, not really. I haven’t noticed a strong pattern of not enjoying things I used to enjoy. If it’s there, it’s subtle enough that I’m not really identifying it as a separate problem.
Over the past two weeks, have you felt down, depressed, or hopeless most of the time?

Not most of the time, no. I mean, I’ve had moments where I feel kind of discouraged or worn down, but I wouldn’t describe the last two weeks as me feeling down or hopeless most of the day, nearly every day, if that’s what you mean.

I’m trying to be accurate, because “down” can mean a lot of things. There are definitely times where I feel frustrated with myself or like I’m not keeping up the way I should, and that can put me in a bad mood. But depressed or hopeless feels stronger than what I’ve noticed. I don’t think I’ve been waking up feeling like everything is bleak, or carrying that feeling around all day.

So I’d say no, not really. Maybe occasional low mood or discouragement, but not most of the time over the past two weeks.

The absence of significant mood changes, anhedonia, or other depressive features rules out most depressive disorder codes (F32.0, F32.1, F32.2, F32.3, F32.8, F32.9). The pattern is more consistent with ADHD, predominantly inattentive presentation, which is coded as F90.0.

opening_question.question: Hello, welcome to the clinic. I'm Dr. [Name]. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient presents with persistent difficulties in attention, organization, and task completion across multiple domains (work, home), with associated restlessness and frustration, but without significant mood symptoms or anxiety sufficient to meet criteria for other disorders. These symptoms are consistent with ADHD, predominantly inattentive presentation.
